name: Ahinadab
title: Solomon's district governor in Mahanaim
lifespan: Unknown, active during Solomon's reign (c. 960–930 BC)
summary: Ahinadab, son of Iddo, was one of the twelve district governors appointed by King Solomon to manage provisions for the royal court. His area of responsibility was the Mahanaim district in Transjordan, a region with deep historical significance – the place where Jacob met God’s angels, where Ish-bosheth established his royal seat, and where David found refuge during Absalom's rebellion. As part of a rotation system, Ahinadab was responsible for supplying the royal household with provisions one month each year, a task that demanded great organizational skill and resource management. That Solomon placed a trusted governor in this strategically important border region east of the Jordan testifies to a well-considered national administration that secured control over the entire territory of the united kingdom.

keyEvents.title: Appointment as district governor in Mahanaim
keyEvents.description: Ahinadab, son of Iddo, was appointed by King Solomon as one of twelve district governors responsible for the Mahanaim region. This strategically important area east of the Jordan had a rich history as a place of refuge and an administrative center.

keyEvents.title: Part of Solomon's administrative supply system
keyEvents.description: As a district governor, Ahinadab was part of an organized rotation system in which twelve governors took turns supplying the royal household with food, one month each. The system required daily deliveries of large quantities of flour, meat, and fodder to the royal court and its stables.

versions.reason: [minor] The role 'leader' is very general. A more precise role would be 'district governor' or 'official', which better describes Ahinadab's specific function in Solomon's administration.; [minor] The four key events overlap significantly. Event 1 and 2 both refer to 1 Kings 4:14 and in practice describe the same appointment. Events 3 and 4 both concern the supply system. These could have been consolidated into fewer, more distinct events.; [minor] Iddo as Ahinadab's father: There are several people named Iddo in the OT. It should be noted that this is likely not the same Iddo as the prophet or other well-known figures named Iddo. The value 'iddo' is correct as a reference, but it is worth being aware of possible confusion.; [major] Footnotes are missing. A profile should have footnotes covering historical, archaeological, or linguistic details, for example about the meaning of Mahanaim, the administrative system, or the etymology of the name.

versions.summary: Ahinadab was the son of Iddo and one of King Solomon's twelve district governors responsible for providing food to the royal household. He was in charge of the district of Mahanaim in Transjordan, an important administrative and strategic area east of the Jordan. Mahanaim had previously served as a refuge for King David during Absalom's rebellion, and the appointment of a district governor there testifies to the site's continued significance in the united kingdom.

Consider removing verse 7 or keeping only verses that are directly relevant (v. 14 for Ahinadab, vv. 22–23 and 27–28 for the general supply system).; [minor] The summary is well written, but given that this is version 2, it should differ more from version 1. The current text has a very similar structure and wording to the previous version. A clearer rephrasing would strengthen the profile.; [minor] The lifespan of approximately 970–930 BC is reasonable for an official under Solomon, but it is worth noting that this is highly speculative. His active period as district governor may have been shorter than Solomon's entire reign. A formulation such as 'active circa 960–930 BC' or 'unknown, active during Solomon's reign' could be more precise.

versions.summary: Ahinadab, son of Iddo, served as one of twelve district governors under King Solomon. His area of responsibility was the Mahanaim district in Transjordan, a region with deep historical resonance – the place where Jacob met angels, where Ish-bosheth held court, and where David sought refuge during Absalom's rebellion. As part of Solomon's supply system, Ahinadab was obligated to provide for the royal household one month each year, an assignment that required considerable resources and administrative capacity. His appointment to this strategically important border region underscores Solomon's desire to secure control over the entire kingdom, including the eastern territories.

footnotes.text: The name Ahinadab (Hebrew: אֲחִינָדָב, 'Achinadav') likely means 'my brother is noble' or 'brother of generosity,' composed of 'ach' (brother) and 'nadav' (noble/willing). The name element 'nadav' also appears in other biblical names such as Nadab and Aminadab.

Mahanaim (Hebrew: מַחֲנַיִם, 'two camps') was a city east of the Jordan with great historical significance. It is first mentioned in Gen 32:2, where Jacob gave it that name after meeting God's angels. It later served as the capital for Ish-bosheth (2 Sam 2:8–9) and as a refuge for David during Absalom's rebellion (2 Sam 17:24–27).

Solomon's division of the kingdom into twelve administrative districts represented a significant bureaucratic innovation in Israel. The division did not follow traditional tribal boundaries, which may have been a deliberate attempt to centralize power and weaken the political influence of the tribes. Each district was to supply the royal household for one month of the year.

Archaeological finds from the Transjordan region, including administrative buildings and storehouses, confirm that the area around Mahanaim was an important administrative center in the Iron Age. The exact location of Mahanaim is still debated among scholars, but Tell ed-Dhahab el-Gharbi by the Jabbok River is a leading candidate.

Ahinadab's father Iddo (Hebrew: עִדּוֹ) should not be confused with other biblical figures of the same name, such as the prophet Iddo (2 Chr 9:29) or the Levite son Iddo (1 Chr 6:21). The name may be linked to the Hebrew root עדה, possibly meaning 'to adorn' or 'to distinguish oneself.'

It is worth noting that several of Solomon's district governors are identified as sons-in-law of the king (1 Kgs 4:11, 15), underscoring that these offices were tied to political alliances. Ahinadab is not mentioned with such a relationship, but his father's name Iddo may suggest he came from a family with an administrative background.
